It is very hot in Germany. Temperatures are above 38 degrees. This is a record for April. Many people drink lots of water and stay at home.

The heat is a problem. Older people and small children are in danger. The fire service has received many emergency calls. The hospitals are full.

The German Weather Service says: The heat will stay for another three days. Then rain will come. People should stay out of the sun and drink plenty of water.

Germany is experiencing an unusual heatwave. Temperatures above 38 degrees were measured in several federal states. April has not been this warm for 145 years. The German Weather Service has issued an official heat warning.

Older people and children are particularly affected. In many cities, outdoor swimming pools have opened earlier than planned. Schools have shortened lessons because classrooms were too hot. Some local authorities have set up cooling rooms.

Experts explain that extreme weather events like these are becoming more common because climate change is raising temperatures. The federal government has announced stronger heat protection plans.

A heatwave unprecedented for April has swept across Germany. Temperatures of up to 39.4 degrees were recorded in parts of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, levels previously seen only in high summer. The German Weather Service classified the situation in twelve federal states as a health hazard.

The consequences are far-reaching: numerous railway lines were closed because tracks overheated, and emergency departments recorded a sharp increase in cases of heat-related collapse. Particularly vulnerable groups, including people needing care and people experiencing homelessness, are the focus of relief measures.

Climate researchers at the Potsdam Institute stress that human-caused climate change has made events of this kind statistically up to twenty times more likely. The federal government is under pressure to overhaul national heat protection plans.

The April 2026 heatwave has placed Germany in an exceptional situation meteorologically and ruthlessly exposed structural shortcomings in its handling of climate-related extremes. With peak temperatures reaching 39.7 degrees, the event eclipsed every measurement record since systematic weather observations began.

While countries such as France established comprehensive national heat protection plans following the devastating heatwave of 2003, Germany still lacks a binding legal framework requiring local authorities to establish cooling centres or release heat-exposed employees from work. This failure is political rather than technical.

The situation in care is particularly alarming. Mortality rates demonstrably rose during the heatwave in poorly air-conditioned residential and nursing homes, a finding that has so far attracted little attention in public debate.

The heatwave is therefore more than a weather event: it is a stress test for the welfare state, raising the question of whom it protects in extreme situations and whom it does not.

Many trains in Germany are late. This is a big problem. Deutsche Bahn says: In March 2026, one in three long-distance trains was late. Many people are very unhappy.

Why are trains late? There are many old tracks and old stations. Sometimes the weather also causes problems. Repairs take a long time.

Deutsche Bahn wants to solve the problem. It is investing a lot of money in new tracks. But the work will take many years. Passengers will have to wait a long time yet.

Deutsche Bahn reported its worst punctuality figures in three years in the first quarter of 2026. Only 67 per cent of long-distance trains arrived on time. This means one in three trains was more than six minutes late.

The main reasons are poor infrastructure and a lack of capacity on busy lines. Frequent construction work also slows services down. Passenger associations have described the situation as unacceptable.

The federal government has promised to invest more than 40 billion euros in the rail network by 2030. However, critics say this is too little and too slow. Many commuters have now switched to cars.

With a long-distance punctuality rate of 67.3 per cent, Deutsche Bahn set a new negative record in the first quarter of 2026. By comparison, Swiss Federal Railways consistently achieves more than 92 per cent. The gap is symptomatic of the state of Germany's railway network.

The maintenance backlog is the central problem. Decades of underinvestment mean that thousands of kilometres of track now need to be renewed simultaneously, a process that severely disrupts existing services. An acute shortage of skilled staff adds to the problem: around 5,000 train driver positions remain vacant.

A study by the German Institute for Economic Research puts the economic cost of train delays at more than four billion euros annually. Deutsche Bahn is announcing a complete overhaul of its most important corridors, but initial results are not expected before 2028.

Deutsche Bahn's chronic lack of punctuality is not a technical failure: it is the result of decades of misguided structural decisions. A punctuality rate of 67 per cent shows that a company oriented towards stock-market returns and an infrastructure mission serving the public good are compatible only to a limited extent.

The core problem lies in the ownership structure. As a federally owned group, DB faces pressure to generate returns, embedded in its corporate culture since the 1990s. At the same time, it is supposed to guarantee nationwide mobility, including on commercially unprofitable routes in disadvantaged regions.

There is also a staffing paradox largely ignored by politicians: while Deutsche Bahn makes high-profile announcements of multibillion-euro programmes for new trains, it simply lacks the drivers to operate them.

Germany needs a clear separation between network and operations, secure long-term infrastructure funding, and the political courage to treat mobility as a public good rather than a market product.

There are fewer and fewer bees in Germany. This is very bad. Bees are very important for nature. They help flowers and fruit trees grow.

Why are bees dying? There are too many pesticides in farming. These are poisonous to bees. Climate change is also a problem. Flowers bloom too early, and bees cannot find food.

What can we do? Many people now plant flowers in their gardens for bees. The government wants to allow fewer pesticides. This is good for nature.

German beekeepers are reporting alarming losses. According to the German Beekeepers' Association, around 20 per cent of all bee colonies in Germany did not survive the winter of 2025/2026. This is one of the highest figures in years.

The causes are complex. Agricultural pesticides weaken bees' immune systems. The Varroa mite, a parasite, attacks colonies and is difficult to control. Climate change adds to the problem: mild winters help diseases spread.

Without bees there is no pollination, and without pollination there is no fruit. Experts estimate that a third of our food depends on pollination by insects. Environmental organisations are calling for stricter rules on crop protection products.

In its latest annual report, the German Beekeepers' Association documented colony losses of almost 21 per cent for the winter of 2025/2026, a figure that concerns specialists and has reignited a broad debate about the state of Germany's agricultural landscape.

The main causes are thought to be an interaction between pesticide exposure, habitat loss and climate change. Neonicotinoid insecticides in particular are suspected of permanently damaging bees' ability to navigate. Although the EU imposed a partial ban on these substances in 2018, exemptions continue to be granted.

The economic consequences are considerable: fruit and rapeseed yields have measurably declined in affected regions. Scientists at the University of Hohenheim are calling for a comprehensive national monitoring programme and reform of EU agricultural policy.

The annually documented decline in Germany's bee colonies has long been more than a beekeeping problem: it is a precise indicator of the ecological condition of an agricultural landscape geared for decades towards maximisation rather than resilience.

The scientific evidence is clear: neonicotinoids and other systemic insecticides demonstrably impair bees' learning and orientation, even below acutely toxic concentrations. Land consolidation also removes flowering areas, leaving bees unable to find sufficient food in agricultural regions with little structural diversity.

What the debate systematically overlooks, however, is the political-economic dimension. As long as EU agricultural subsidies are linked primarily to the area farmed rather than ecological services, incentives for insect-friendly farming remain marginal.

The bee is an indicator species. Its disappearance shows that the entire ecosystem is under pressure. A society that ignores this risks more than honey.

It is difficult to find a home in Germany. There are not enough homes, especially in big cities such as Berlin, Munich and Hamburg. Rents are very expensive.

Many people spend a long time looking for a home. Students, young families and people with little money have the biggest problems. Sometimes a hundred people compete for just one flat.

The government wants to build more homes. But building is also very expensive. Experts say: It will take many years to solve the problem.

The housing crisis in Germany's major cities continues to get worse. In Berlin, Munich and Frankfurt, rents rose again last year by an average of eight per cent. At the same time, fewer homes were built in 2025 than in any year for two decades.

There are several reasons. High construction costs, rising interest rates and a shortage of land slow down new building. Many construction companies have stopped projects because they are no longer profitable. The government has missed its target of 400,000 new homes per year by a wide margin.

Families with middle incomes are particularly affected. They earn too much for social housing but too little to pay expensive market rents. Tenants' associations are calling for an immediate programme of affordable housing.

Germany is experiencing its worst housing crisis since the post-war period. With only 215,000 new homes built in 2025, a structural gap is reflected in soaring rents and growing waiting lists for social housing.

The crisis results from a double failure: the market has mainly produced luxury apartments focused on returns, while creating little affordable housing. The state has neglected investment in social housing: the stock has fallen from four million homes in 1990 to fewer than 1.1 million.

Urban researchers warn of increasing social segregation: lower-income households are pushed to the outskirts, while city centres are dominated by wealthier groups. No quick solution is in sight.

Germany's housing crisis is not a natural event but the predictable outcome of decades of deregulation that consistently left housing to market logic. With 215,000 new homes in 2025, the gap between supply and demand has widened so far that market mechanisms alone can no longer close it.

The historical comparison is particularly revealing: in the 1970s, federal, state and local governments still provided more than 30 per cent of newly built homes as subsidised housing. Today that share is below five per cent, the consequence of an ideological decision to define housing as a private consumer good.

The social and spatial consequences are measurable: low earners, single parents and migrants are increasingly concentrated in particular neighbourhoods. Urban sociologists describe residential segregation that threatens social cohesion over the long term.

A structural solution requires housing to be redefined as a public good, with the corresponding institutional, financial and legal consequences. Whether the political will exists remains the decisive question.

The DAX is the most important stock index in Germany. It shows how the 40 biggest German companies are doing on the stock market. In April 2026, the DAX is very high.

When the DAX rises, it means companies have earned a lot of money. Many investors buy shares. This is a good sign for the economy.

But a high DAX does not always mean everyone is doing well. Food and housing prices are still high. This is a contradiction.

Germany's DAX stock index reached a new all-time high in the second week of April 2026. The index of the 40 largest German listed companies climbed above 23,500 points. This record surprised many investors, as Germany's economic situation is still considered difficult.

The main drivers are strong quarterly results from several DAX companies, particularly SAP, Siemens and Allianz. Relief over the ceasefire in the Iran conflict, which stabilised energy prices, also helped. The prospect of further interest rate cuts by the European Central Bank is boosting confidence too.

However, experts warn against excessive optimism. A rising stock index does not necessarily reflect the condition of the whole economy. Domestic demand in Germany remains weak, and many medium-sized companies continue to struggle with high costs.

The DAX broke through 23,500 points this week, setting a new all-time high. The rally is supported by a mixture of stable corporate profits, lower interest rates and geopolitical easing, a combination pushing investors towards riskier assets.

SAP is a particularly important contributor to the index's strength: the Walldorf software group increased its cloud revenue to 21 billion euros in 2025 and is targeting free cash flow of 10 billion euros for 2026. Siemens Energy also benefits from the infrastructure equipment boom, and Rheinmetall ranks among the strongest DAX stocks following the increase in defence spending.

The paradox remains: while the DAX sets records, Germany's economy stagnates. The Ifo business climate has recovered slightly but remains below its long-term average. Small investors considering entering the market now face the classic question: is this still a good time to buy, or the peak before a crash?

An all-time high for the DAX is, depending on perspective, a sign of economic strength or a symptom of structural decoupling. Reality is probably closer to the latter. Germany's leading stock index setting records while domestic demand stagnates, insolvencies among medium-sized businesses reach historic highs, and industrial production declines across large areas reveals a growing separation between market value and economic substance.

The DAX does not represent the German economy: it indexes multinational groups generating most of their revenue abroad. SAP earns in the US, Siemens in Asia and BASF worldwide. A rising DAX therefore primarily signals favourable global demand and international financial conditions, rather than prosperity for Germany as a business location.

The monetary policy situation remains ambiguous. ECB rate cuts make shares relatively more attractive than bonds, a mechanical effect producing price gains without any necessary improvement in companies' operating performance. This TINA logic, meaning There Is No Alternative, pushes capital into equity markets even while fundamentals remain mixed.

For private investors, the record DAX is therefore an invitation to closer analysis rather than an unthinking purchase: what do these companies really earn, and at what price am I buying it?

SAP is a German company. It comes from Walldorf in Baden-Württemberg. SAP makes software for other companies. This is very important for the economy.

SAP is the most valuable company in Germany. This means SAP shares are worth a lot of money. Many investors buy SAP shares.

In 2025, SAP earned a lot of money. Its revenue was a record. Many companies around the world use SAP software.

With a market capitalisation of more than 280 billion euros, SAP is Germany's most valuable company and one of the world's leading software groups. Its success is based on a transformation that began a few years ago: moving from traditional software licences to cloud-based subscription services.

In the 2025 financial year, SAP increased cloud revenue to 21 billion euros, a rise of 23 per cent. Free cash flow almost doubled to 8.2 billion euros. The group has announced even more ambitious targets for 2026.

An important driver is pressure to migrate: around 40 per cent of SAP customers still use old systems that must switch to the new S/4HANA platform by the end of 2027. This guarantees predictable revenue for years. Most analysts recommend buying the shares.

SAP has completed its transformation from a sluggish ERP provider into an agile cloud group, and capital markets are rewarding it impressively. With a market capitalisation exceeding 280 billion euros, SAP now surpasses even Volkswagen, Siemens and Deutsche Telekom combined. This would have been unthinkable just five years ago.

The strategic core of the transformation is the cloud. SAP increasingly offers business applications, from accounting and human resources to supply chains, as subscription services. This reduces one-off payments but creates stable, recurring revenue. Its cloud order backlog of 77 billion euros indicates the reliability of these earnings.

There is also a structural advantage: the compulsory migration from legacy systems to S/4HANA by 2027 ties millions of business customers to SAP, regardless of competition and the economic cycle. A critical question remains whether SAP can compete in AI against American platform providers such as Microsoft or Salesforce. The answer will determine its next growth phase.

SAP is an anomaly in Germany's economic landscape. While the country's core industrial sectors, automotive, chemicals and engineering, struggle with structural challenges, the Walldorf software group has created value over the past five years that is difficult to match in European technology. Its market capitalisation exceeding 280 billion euros surpasses the combined value of all DAX automotive groups.

SAP's rise is explained not by a technological revolution but by a strategic reversal: the determined shift from one-off licence sales to recurring cloud revenue. The transformation was painful, initially depressing margins, but created a quality of earnings that capital markets systematically value more highly than cyclical industrial profits.

For Germany as a business location, SAP also sends an ambiguous signal. The group employs more than 105,000 people worldwide, around a third of them in Germany. It pays taxes, invests in research and provides training, but its business model is fundamentally global and data-based rather than local and production-based. SAP benefits from German engineering culture but cannot guarantee the country's industrial future.

The real question is whether Germany can produce a second SAP or whether this group will remain a historical stroke of luck.

Anthropic is a company from the US. It makes artificial intelligence. Its best-known product is called Claude. Many people use Claude every day.

Anthropic wants to go public. This means ordinary people will be able to buy Anthropic shares. The company is worth a lot of money.

AI companies are very interesting to investors at the moment. Everyone wants to invest in artificial intelligence. This is a big trend.

According to insiders, the American AI company Anthropic, developer of the Claude assistant, plans to go public later this year. The IPO, or Initial Public Offering, could value the company at more than 60 billion US dollars, making it one of the largest stock market listings in recent history.

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees. It presents itself as a safety-focused AI developer and has created one of the world's most widely used AI applications in Claude. Major investors such as Google and Amazon have already invested billions in the company.

For German investors, the possible IPO is an important event: AI shares are currently among the most sought-after investments. Those wanting an early investment in technology companies riding the AI wave are watching Anthropic's listing closely.

Anthropic's planned stock market listing would take place in an environment valuing AI companies at unprecedented multiples. A valuation exceeding 60 billion US dollars would imply a price-to-sales ratio that looks ambitious even for growth companies: Anthropic most recently generated annual revenue of around 2.5 billion US dollars.

What distinguishes Anthropic from competitors such as OpenAI is its explicit positioning as a safety company. Its concept of constitution-based AI development and focus on AI safety have brought both scientific credibility and strategic advantages in regulatory discussions.

Capital markets face three core questions: how sustainable is revenue growth in an increasingly competitive market? How heavily does the business model depend on a handful of large customers? And how will valuation logic change as regulation of AI systems becomes stricter? The IPO prospectus will have to provide answers.

Anthropic's possible IPO is more than a financial market event: it is a stress test for valuation logic across the AI sector. A company valuation above 60 billion US dollars on annual revenue of around 2.5 billion implies a price-to-sales ratio of 24, a figure justified only by exceptional growth and structural market power even in a low-interest-rate environment.

Anthropic's distinguishing feature, AI safety at the core of its business model rather than as a marketing addition, is strategically well positioned. As regulators worldwide develop safety standards for AI systems, a company treating compliance and safety architecture as competitive advantages enjoys structural benefits. The EU AI Act, the US executive-order regime and comparable Asian frameworks are likely to favour providers with robust safety documentation.

The structural risk lies elsewhere: in the capital intensity of training frontier models, dependence on a small number of cloud infrastructure providers, and whether language models establish enduring platform dynamics or become commodities where the lowest-priced provider wins.

For investors, Anthropic is a high-risk investment in the institutionalisation of AI, with genuine upside potential but no historical precedent.

Defence companies make weapons and military products. One example in Germany is Rheinmetall. Rheinmetall shares are very expensive at the moment.

Why are defence shares rising? Countries in Europe are spending more money on their militaries. This is because of wars around the world. More military spending means more orders for defence companies.

Some people think investing money in defence shares is a problem. Others say it is necessary for Europe's security. This is a difficult debate.

Hardly any industry has risen as strongly on the stock market over the past two years as defence. Shares in Rheinmetall, Germany's largest defence group, have increased more than tenfold since 2022. European competitors such as Leonardo, BAE Systems and Thales are also recording all-time highs.

The main reason is clear: European countries are greatly increasing defence spending. Germany has approved a special fund of 100 billion euros for the armed forces. NATO countries aim to meet the two-per-cent target. These investments mean long-term orders for defence companies.

However, this also raises ethical questions. More investors are asking whether defence investment is compatible with sustainable investment strategies. Some funds have excluded defence shares from their ESG portfolios, while others have explicitly included them.

The rally in European defence shares has structural support. Rheinmetall, the Düsseldorf-based tank and ammunition manufacturer, has increased its order backlog to more than 50 billion euros, several times its annual revenue. The predictability of these earnings over many years is highly attractive to institutional investors.

The driver is Europe's new defence reality. With its 100-billion-euro special fund and intended two-per-cent target, Germany has undergone a paradigm shift. France, Poland and the Baltic states have also substantially expanded military budgets. For defence companies, this means decades of secure orders.

The other side is the ESG debate. Sustainability-focused investors face a dilemma: traditional ESG criteria frequently exclude defence as a sector. In the current security context, however, several EU institutions have begun classifying defence investment as necessary to preserve democratic societies, a reassessment presenting unfamiliar questions for the ESG industry.

The defence boom on European stock markets presents sustainable finance with a conceptual breaking point. For years the principle was that defence companies are by definition incompatible with ESG criteria: they manufacture weapons, instruments of destruction. This view was morally comfortable and analytically simple. Given Europe's changed security reality, it increasingly seems a luxury.

The argument made by defence supporters runs as follows: a society that loses its defensive capability also loses the foundation for all other sustainability goals. Democratic institutions, the rule of law and social security require physical security. In a specific historical context, defence investment is therefore investment in the preconditions for sustainability.

This argument has gaps. It abstracts from the question of which weapons are supplied to which countries for which purposes. A supplier simultaneously equipping authoritarian regimes can hardly be classified as ESG-compliant. Distinguishing defensive from offensive weapons, and democratic customer states from others, is analytically possible but requires transparency that many defence companies have yet to offer.

What remains is the uncomfortable recognition that capital markets and geopolitics are not separate spheres, and that every investment decision contains an implicit worldview.

Interrail is a train ticket for Europe. With this ticket, you can travel by train in many countries. It is one ticket for all trains.

Many young people buy an Interrail ticket for the summer holidays. It is a cheap way to travel. You can visit Paris, Rome or Barcelona.

This year, especially many teenagers are buying the ticket. Trains are good for the environment. Many young people think this is important.

The Interrail ticket is reaching a new record this summer. More than 500,000 young Europeans have already booked it for the summer holidays of 2026, more than ever before. The ticket allows unlimited train travel in 33 European countries.

There are several reasons for the boom. Many teenagers want to travel sustainably and avoid flying. The EU has also offered free Interrail passes for 18-year-olds since 2021. Hundreds of thousands of young people have used this offer in recent years.

Popular destinations include Spain, Italy and Portugal. But less well-known countries such as Slovenia and North Macedonia are also becoming more popular. The train is slower than the plane, but many say the journey itself is the experience.

The Interrail ticket is more popular than ever this summer. More than half a million bookings had already been recorded in April, around 30 per cent more than in the same period last year. Behind the boom lies more than a travel trend: it is a cultural change in how young Europeans think about holidays.

Environmental awareness, the free EU pass for 18-year-olds and growing scepticism towards mass tourism have combined to produce a new generation of rail travellers. Rather than all-inclusive holidays or low-cost flight weekends, slow travel is becoming the guiding principle: travelling consciously, planning stopovers and discovering cities off the tourist trail.

For Deutsche Bahn and its European partners, the boom poses a challenge. Popular routes such as Munich–Venice and Berlin–Prague are often fully booked in summer. The EU is discussing whether to create more night connections and improve cross-border booking infrastructure to support the trend.

The Interrail boom of 2026 is not merely a market phenomenon: it reflects a deeper shift in young Europeans' travel culture. Someone travelling from Berlin to Lisbon by train today makes a decision charged with ecological, political and aesthetic significance: travelling more slowly, emitting less, and experiencing Europe as a landscape rather than an airspace.

The EU has actively encouraged this change. Its DiscoverEU programme, which provides free Interrail passes to 18-year-olds, is conceptually astute: it combines support for mobility with the formation of European identity. A teenager who has travelled through ten countries by train has encountered Europe as a lived space rather than an abstract political project.

Structurally, however, the boom exposes deficiencies in Europe's rail network. Cross-border bookings remain cumbersome, night connections are scarce, and fares outside the Interrail pass struggle to compete with low-cost airlines. Whether Europe acquires a genuine twenty-first-century rail network ultimately depends on political will and willingness to invest, rather than demand. The demand clearly exists.

Interrail is thus more than a ticket. It is an argument.

There are many surf camps on the Baltic Sea in northern Germany. Children and teenagers learn to surf there. Surfing is a lot of fun.

The Baltic Sea is calmer than the Atlantic. This is good for beginners. You can also learn kitesurfing, stand-up paddleboarding and windsurfing.

In summer, many teenagers come from all over Germany. They stay at the camp, eat together and make new friends. It is a great experience.

Surf camps on the Baltic coasts of Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg report many fully booked weeks for summer 2026. Demand for water sports holidays in Germany has risen strongly in recent years, particularly among teenagers aged 13 to 19.

At the camps, participants can learn windsurfing, kitesurfing, SUP, or stand-up paddleboarding, and traditional wave surfing. The Baltic Sea is ideal for beginners because its waves are lower. Experienced surfers can still find real challenges on windy days.

Many teenagers arrive alone and meet new people at camp. For many, the social experience is just as important as the sport itself. Parents appreciate the educational supervision and the considerable freedom the camps offer at the same time.

Booking figures are clear: water sports holiday camps on Germany's Baltic coast are more popular than ever in summer 2026. Operators in Prerow, Kühlungsborn and on Fehmarn report high-season waiting lists and significantly greater domestic demand. Industry specialists attribute the trend to a combination of post-pandemic catch-up effects, higher foreign travel costs and growing interest in outdoor sports.

The offering has become more professional in recent years. Modern camps combine water sports training with sustainable approaches: solar energy, vegetarian meals and local partnerships with organic farmers are now standard for many providers. Some camps have integrated language modules, with English in the morning and surfing in the afternoon.

For many teenagers, these holidays are more than a break. The combination of physical challenge, community and closeness to nature creates experiences rarely available in everyday school life. Educators view such programmes as a valuable complement to leisure habits dominated by digital activities.

The boom in surf camps on Germany's Baltic Sea is unsurprising: it is the predictable result of several converging trends. Rising air travel costs, greater awareness of nature-based leisure and the pandemic-driven rediscovery of domestic destinations have more than doubled demand for water sports holiday camps over the past three years.

The educational dimension is as interesting as the economic one. Surf camps promise, and often deliver, something increasingly rare in teenagers' daily lives: physical challenges in a non-competitive setting, direct encounters with nature without digital mediation, and social bonds formed through shared effort. Research into positive youth development supports these experiences empirically.

At the same time, the sector is becoming increasingly commercialised, with contradictions of its own. Premium camps offering wellness facilities and influencer partnerships compete for wealthy customers, while cheaper options for lower-income families become rarer. Whether outdoor sports experiences should remain a middle-class privilege or become more accessible through public funding has barely entered political debate.

A surf camp is not an educational programme. But it is not insignificant either.

The Deutschlandticket costs 58 euros a month. With this ticket, you can travel by bus and train all over Germany. It is very practical.

Many teenagers use the ticket in the summer holidays. For example, they travel to the Baltic Sea or the mountains. The ticket is cheap and environmentally friendly.

You can buy the ticket each month and cancel it again. This is very flexible. Young people in particular think the ticket is great.

Since its introduction in 2023, the Deutschlandticket has been one of Germany's most successful local transport projects. For 58 euros a month, holders can use all buses, suburban trains, underground trains and regional trains throughout Germany, without extra charges or reservations.

Many teenagers use the ticket for cheap domestic travel, especially during the summer holidays. With the ticket and some patience, you can travel from Munich to the Baltic coast or explore the Black Forest, for example. However, Deutsche Bahn long-distance trains are not included.

Critics argue that the ticket is of little use in disadvantaged regions because public transport services are limited there. The federal states are therefore discussing whether targeted investment in rural local transport should accompany it. For city residents, by contrast, it is a real alternative to the car.

The Deutschlandticket celebrates its third birthday this summer, and its record is mixed. The positives include more than 13 million subscribers, a measurable reduction in car traffic in major cities and increased mobility for lower-income groups. The negatives include unresolved funding and structurally incomplete local transport provision in rural regions.

For teenagers, the ticket is a real game changer in summer. Several federal states offer discounted or free versions for school pupils. Those who are flexible and accept connection times can explore much of Germany cheaply. Travellers describe spontaneous discoveries: cities that would have remained out of reach with an expensive train ticket.

However, the ticket's political future is uncertain. Federal and state governments have argued over funding for months. Ending the offer would affect millions of subscribers and send a signal: political willingness to transform mobility reaches its limits when money is involved.

The Deutschlandticket is the most ambitious and simultaneously most contradictory transport policy project in recent German history. In three years, it has brought more people onto local public transport than all the campaigns and funding programmes of preceding decades, yet remains permanently precarious because its financing has never been fundamentally resolved politically.

The structural tension is evident: the ticket is neutral regarding geography and service provision. It makes mobility cheaper where good services already exist and changes little where buses run once a day or not at all. Residents of Munich or Hamburg benefit enormously. Residents of the Altmark or Eifel gain little from a cheap ticket if the next bus arrives three hours later. The ticket does not resolve the network question: it presupposes an answer.

For young people, nevertheless, the offer is transformative. It permits an experimental approach to mobility: spontaneous, station-based and exploratory. A 17-year-old travelling through Germany on regional trains experiences the country in a way neither cars nor aircraft provide. In this sense, the Deutschlandticket is also a cultural policy instrument, whether its creators realised it or not.

The real question is whether Germany is willing to fund this instrument permanently. So far, the answer is renegotiated annually, which means unresolved.

Many young people work at holiday camps in the summer holidays. They look after children and teenagers. It is a great summer job.

Camp leaders do not earn much money. But they get accommodation and food. They learn a lot and make new friends.

You must be at least 18 years old. A first aid course is often necessary. Many university students do this job during their holidays.

Every year, youth travel companies in Germany look for thousands of leaders for their summer camps. This is not a typical holiday job: it is intense, responsible work and also one of the most varied experiences you can have at 20.

Camp leaders are responsible for a group of children or teenagers around the clock. They organise activities, solve conflicts, look after safety and make sure everyone has a good time. Pay is low, often just pocket money plus accommodation and meals. But the experience gained is hard to put a price on.

Many camp leaders report that the job changed their personality. They learned to take responsibility, be patient and lead groups. These skills are very valuable later in education and employment.

Germany's holiday camp market is growing, along with demand for qualified camp leaders. Major operators such as ruf Jugendreisen, Freebird and the AWO youth organisation seek more than 10,000 seasonal workers between them each year for summer programmes. Many providers report that demand exceeds supply.

The job requires more than a good mood. In addition to a minimum age of 18, a first aid course, experience working with children and teenagers and often English skills are usually required. Leaders at international camps need intercultural competence. Major operators provide several days of training before summer.

Financially, the job is not very attractive: pocket money ranges from 200 to 400 euros per week, plus free accommodation and meals. Nevertheless, many applicants are attracted by the combination of adventure, community and a feeling of being genuinely needed. Recruitment managers report that many former leaders describe the job as one of their youth's most formative experiences.

Holiday camps rarely feature in discussions of informal learning and skills development outside school. Yet they offer one of the most concentrated environments for what educational researchers call transformative experience: a context in which young people take real responsibility, can fail and still receive support.

Someone spending a summer looking after 15 teenagers, mediating arguments, supporting them through low moods, channelling their enthusiasm and regularly feeling overwhelmed themselves, learns more about leadership, communication and empathy than in many seminars. This is not romanticisation but a well-supported empirical proposition: studies of social-emotional skills development consistently show that intensive group responsibility is a particularly effective form of learning.

Nevertheless, society continues to underestimate the camp leader's job. Low pay signals that work with children and teenagers receives little economic value, a pattern repeated throughout the care economy. Someone who spends a summer caring for children performs socially valuable work and receives pocket money for it.

Perhaps this is the job's real lesson: not just what one learns, but also what society is willing to pay for this work.

The Eurovision Song Contest is a big music competition in Europe. Many countries compete by singing. The audience and a jury choose the winner.

This year, Eurovision takes place in Vienna. This is the capital of Austria. Austria won the competition because an Austrian artist won in 2025.

Eurovision is a lot of fun. Millions of people watch the competition on television. Many Germans, Swiss and Austrians are fans too.

This year Vienna hosts the 70th Eurovision Song Contest. Following Austrian artist JJ's victory last year, Austria received the right to organise the competition. The final takes place on 16 May at the Wiener Stadthalle.

More than 37 countries are taking part, including Germany, Switzerland and Austria itself. Each country sends an act with its own song. Voting combines jury decisions with votes from audiences across Europe.

Vienna expects hundreds of thousands of visitors. The city has planned an extensive programme of related events: free open-air concerts, fan zones and a Eurovision exhibition at the Museum of Art History. For the tourism industry, it is the most important event of the year.

The 70th Eurovision Song Contest, whose final takes place at the Wiener Stadthalle on 16 May, has long been more than a song competition. It is an annual ritual of European identity, a platform for cultural self-presentation and, for years, an increasingly politically charged event.

Austria welcomes the contest's return to Vienna, where it last took place in 2015. Hosting brings considerable revenue: experts estimate an economic effect exceeding 200 million euros for the Vienna urban region. Hotels have been fully booked for months, and demand for tickets exceeded supply within minutes.

For Germany, Eurovision is a special matter. After years of poor results, including several last places, broadcaster NDR has reformed the selection process and is backing an act in 2026 that already has a strong social media fan base. Whether this is enough to overcome the stigma of Germany's Eurovision failures will become clear in May.

The Eurovision Song Contest is European cultural policy's best-kept paradox: an explicitly apolitical competition that has functioned for decades as a seismograph for political tensions, social change and national self-images. Its 70th edition in Vienna adds another chapter to this paradox.

What began as a post-war radio format, a technical experiment in practising European broadcasting cooperation, has become the world's largest annual television event, with up to 200 million viewers. Its reach exceeds that of most major sporting events. Eurovision is therefore also a political stage: voting between neighbouring countries reveals geopolitical proximity, Russia's exclusion in 2022 was a cultural policy statement, and Israel's participation despite the ongoing conflict sparks debate each year.

For Austria, hosting is a balancing act. Vienna wants to present itself as an open-minded, tolerant metropolis while also handling demonstrations and political opposition. Eurovision forces its host city to adopt positions it would prefer to avoid.

Ultimately, Eurovision is what Europe itself is: inconsistent, noisy, occasionally absurd and astonishingly resilient.

There is a new sports competition in Las Vegas. It is called the Enhanced Games. Athletes can use doping in this competition. This is forbidden in other competitions.

The organisers say: Doping is everywhere anyway. It is better if it is open and safe. Doctors should monitor the athletes.

Many people think this is wrong. They say sport should be fair. Others find it interesting. What do you think?

The Enhanced Games have begun in Las Vegas, a privately organised sports competition where performance-enhancing substances are explicitly allowed. Athletes from different disciplines compete without having to fear doping tests.

The founders argue that doping is already widespread in elite sport but takes place in secret. Their idea is that athletes using substances transparently under medical supervision would be safer than the existing system. Critics see this as dangerous normalisation.

The International Olympic Committee and the world athletics federation have strongly condemned the Enhanced Games. Participating athletes risk lifetime bans from Olympic competitions. Nevertheless, several former professional athletes have signed up, attracted by promises of high prize money.

The Enhanced Games, taking place in Las Vegas since this week, are, depending on perspective, a brazen provocation of organised sport, a consistent business model or a radical thought experiment. Permitted doping under medical supervision sounds like satire, but it is deadly serious.

The project's founder, Australian entrepreneur Aron D'Souza, argues from a libertarian perspective: adult athletes should decide for themselves what to do with their bodies. He says the existing anti-doping system is hypocritical because it effectively makes elite sport impossible without substance-based support. This position is provocative but not without empirical foundation.

Established sport reacted predictably: bans, condemnations and distancing. What nevertheless makes the Enhanced Games interesting is the question they raise: to what extent can the existing anti-doping system actually create equal conditions, and how honest is sport with itself?

In their purest provocative form, the Enhanced Games answer a question organised sport has avoided for decades: what exactly should the anti-doping system protect, athletes' health, fairness in competition or sport's commercial image?

The uncomfortable truth is that all three goals are currently inadequately fulfilled. Athletes' health is endangered by a system that prohibits doping while structurally encouraging it through pressure for maximum performance. Fairness is almost impossible in a global system with enormous differences in resources, access to sports medicine and national support structures. Sport's commercial image suffers less from doping than from doping being discovered.

D'Souza's project may not be viable in its present form: the absence of established stars, legal uncertainties and mainstream moral rejection limit its reach. What it does achieve, however, is forcing a debate systematically avoided by institutional sport: about bodily autonomy, the limits of state regulation in sport, and whether an elite athlete taking substances consciously and with full information needs protection from themselves or should be respected.

Sport has no answers yet. The Enhanced Games at least force it to hear the questions.

Many Indigenous peoples live in Brazil. They have lived in the country for thousands of years. Now thousands of them have protested in the capital, Brasília.

They want the government to recognise their territories. These territories are their home and very important to them. But the government often does not give them these lands.

The protest is called Acampamento Terra Livre, which means Free Land Camp. It takes place every year. This year, especially many people came.

Around 8,000 Indigenous people from across Brazil travelled to the capital, Brasília, in early April to demonstrate for recognition of their ancestral territories at the 22nd Acampamento Terra Livre, or Free Land Camp. It is one of the largest Indigenous protests in the country's history.

Their central demand is legal protection of their territories against exploitation by agricultural and mining industries. Many Indigenous communities report illegal logging, poisoned rivers and violent displacement. In the October elections, the movement wants to support candidates who represent its interests.

Germany and the EU are watching closely, because the EU–Mercosur trade agreement will be judged against human rights standards in Brazil, including the rights of Indigenous peoples.

The 22nd Acampamento Terra Livre in Brasília carries particular political significance this year. Around 8,000 participants from more than 200 Indigenous peoples are demanding the constitutionally guaranteed demarcation of their territories and announcing a targeted campaign strategy for October's parliamentary and gubernatorial elections.

The background is an unfulfilled constitutional guarantee: although Brazil's 1988 constitution guarantees Indigenous peoples the right to their ancestral lands, thousands of these territories remain officially undemarcated. Consequently, illegal logging, gold mining and agribusiness encroach on protected areas, often without criminal consequences.

For Europe, the situation matters beyond humanitarian concerns. The planned EU–Mercosur agreement includes sustainability clauses to be assessed against Brazil's environmental and human rights standards. Indigenous organisations and European NGOs demand that territorial demarcation become a condition for trade privileges.

The Acampamento Terra Livre has long been more than a national protest: it is an intersection of global debates about climate protection, colonial legacies and the credibility of international trade relations. That 8,000 Indigenous people from more than 200 peoples must demonstrate in Brasília for their land rights reflects a failure of Brazil's rule of law and the contradictions of global climate policy.

Large parts of the Amazon rainforest, whose protection is a priority in international climate agreements, are guarded by Indigenous communities with little legal recourse against intruders without state recognition of their territories. The paradox is obvious: the world wants to protect the rainforest while its most effective guardians fight for land rights that have long existed on paper.

The European dimension intensifies this paradox. The EU–Mercosur agreement, negotiated for decades, includes sustainability chapters, but enforcement remains weak and oversight inadequate. Indigenous organisations demand structural conditions rather than handouts: no trade privileges without progress on demarcation, and no soybean imports from illegally cleared land.

The protest in Brasília therefore also poses a question to Europe: how much is climate conscience worth if it ends at the boundaries of one's own economic interests?

BTS is a very famous K-pop group from South Korea. They have many fans around the world. These fans are called ARMY.

After a break, BTS is back. They have a new album. They are also doing a big world tour. Germany is on the tour schedule too.

K-pop is music from Korea. It is very popular with young people. The singers dance a lot and wear special costumes. It is a big phenomenon.

South Korean band BTS has announced its return after a two-year break caused by the members' military service. A new album and world tour are planned, with concerts in Seoul, Tokyo, Los Angeles and several European cities, including Berlin.

BTS is more than a music group. In recent years, the seven singers have built a global fan community called ARMY, estimated to have more than 50 million active members. Their music mixes pop, hip-hop and electronic elements, often with lyrics about self-discovery, mental health and social pressure.

K-pop is now a major economic factor for South Korea. Music exports, merchandise and tourism revenue from fans worldwide, known as K-pop tourists, bring the country billions annually. Germany is one of the most important European markets.

BTS's return after its members completed military service is an event of rare significance in the pop world. Few groups have maintained such an intense relationship with fans through a forced break, demonstrating the depth of emotional attachment K-pop acts build with their audiences.

An industrial logic lies behind the phenomenon. Since the 1990s, South Korea has systematically invested in training entertainers and marketing Korean pop culture globally, under the concept of the Korean Wave, or Hallyu. What began as state-supported cultural exports has developed into an autonomous global market encompassing music, fashion, cosmetics, film and language.

For Germany, K-pop also reflects changing cultural consumption. A generation of young people primarily consumes pop culture through social media, regardless of language boundaries and traditional radio formats. A Korean-language group filling sold-out arenas in Frankfurt and Berlin would have been unthinkable twenty years ago.

BTS's return marks a moment extending beyond musical taste. It illustrates the fundamental shift in global pop culture over the past two decades, from Anglo-American dominance to a multipolar market where Southeast Asian, Latin American and African productions develop independent global reach.

South Korea's success is not accidental but the result of consistent cultural policy. Targeted support for entertainment companies, idol training through an industrialised system and early use of digital platforms have created an industry generating more than 12 billion US dollars annually. Hallyu, the Korean Wave, is therefore both soft power and economic strategy.

What is often overlooked is the system's ambivalence. Training conditions in K-pop agencies are strict, sometimes burdensome, and idols' privacy is structurally restricted. The authenticity fans experience is partly the product of sophisticated image production. This tension is not new to the pop industry, but it is particularly visible in K-pop.

BTS have managed to develop their own artistic voice within this system. Their lyrics on mental health, social pressure and self-acceptance strike a chord worldwide, in Korean. That, perhaps, is what is truly revolutionary.

A new study shows that many young people in Germany are very stressed. They are afraid of the future. These are the results of the 2026 youth study.

Thirty per cent of young people need psychological help. This is a record. Their biggest worries are war, housing prices and the economy.

Forty-one per cent of 14- to 29-year-olds are thinking about leaving Germany. They want to live in another country. This is an important signal for politicians.

The new trend study “Youth in Germany 2026: The Future Under Pressure” presents a worrying picture. Around 2,000 young people aged 14 to 29 were interviewed. The result: psychological stress, financial worries and doubts about the future shape many young people's daily lives.

Particularly striking is that 41 per cent of respondents can imagine preferring to live in another country in future. The main reasons given are housing shortages, uncertain job prospects and the general political climate.

Youth researcher Klaus Hurrelmann of the Hertie School in Berlin calls for greater political participation by young people. Society must put more trust in the younger generation, otherwise it risks lasting political alienation.

The ninth edition of the “Youth in Germany” trend study provides alarming findings. One in three of the 2,012 respondents aged 14 to 29 says they need psychological support, a historic high. Their main concerns are wars in Europe and the Middle East, at 62 per cent, expensive housing, at 58 per cent, and economic uncertainty.

The increased willingness to emigrate is particularly notable. Forty-one per cent of young Germans can imagine living abroad permanently, compared with fewer than 25 per cent five years ago. Alongside housing shortages, a main motivation is the feeling of not being heard politically in Germany.

Educational researcher Nina Kolleck of the University of Potsdam sees the findings as a political wake-up call: young people are disappointed rather than apathetic. Anyone wanting to win them back must create genuine forms of participation rather than symbolic policies.

The “Youth in Germany 2026” trend study is more than a report on sentiment: it is a structural diagnosis. That 41 per cent of 14- to 29-year-olds seriously consider emigration primarily indicates collective experiences rather than individual dissatisfaction: housing shortages, labour market insecurity, political exclusion and accumulated perceptions of crisis that have not subsided since the pandemic.

The mental health finding is particularly revealing. Thirty per cent of respondents report needing psychological support, a figure that structurally challenges the capacity of Germany's healthcare system. Waiting six to eighteen months for therapy is a reality in many regions. Demand is growing; provision is not.

The study also shows that the frequently cited political apathy of young people is a misdiagnosis. The data suggest the opposite: a strong awareness of problems combined with deep scepticism about political institutions' ability to solve them. This is rationally grounded alienation rather than indifference.

A society losing 41 per cent of its youngest generation as potential emigrants should ask less what is wrong with its youth, and more what is wrong with their circumstances.

NASA has a new programme. It is called Artemis. The goal is for people to fly to the Moon again. The last time was in 1972.

The rocket is very big and powerful. It is called SLS. The astronauts live in the Orion spacecraft. The journey to the Moon takes several days.

Many children and teenagers find the programme exciting. Perhaps one day a person will also fly to Mars. This is NASA's dream.

NASA's Artemis programme is making progress. Following several test flights, a person is expected to walk on the Moon again in the coming months, for the first time since the Apollo 17 mission in 1972. Particularly historic is the plan for a woman to land on the Moon this time too.

The programme is technically very complex. The SLS rocket is the most powerful NASA has ever built. The Orion spacecraft can carry four astronauts. A small space station called Gateway is also planned near the Moon.

Europe is involved too: the European Space Agency, ESA, developed Orion's service module. For many young people, Artemis shows that space exploration continues and that Mars is getting closer as the next destination.

NASA's Artemis programme is more than a prestige project: it is the foundation for long-term exploration of the solar system. Following the successful uncrewed Artemis I flight in 2022 and the crewed lunar flyby of Artemis II, Artemis III is intended to land humans on the Moon for the first time in more than 50 years, this time near the south pole.

The south pole is particularly interesting scientifically: researchers suspect large quantities of water ice in permanently shadowed craters. Water is important not only for drinking; it could also serve as fuel for future missions. The goal is a permanent human presence on the Moon as a springboard for flights to Mars in the 2040s.

ESA is deeply involved through Orion's service module. Artemis also matters for Germany's industrial policy: German companies such as Airbus Defence and Space supply key components and benefit from the growing space market.

NASA's Artemis programme is, depending on perspective, a scientific milestone, a geopolitical statement or a business model, and in reality all three simultaneously. Returning to the Moon after more than fifty years is not simply a matter of technical capability, but an expression of changed geopolitical circumstances in which the US, China and increasingly Europe compete for influence in near-Earth space.

China has recently explored the lunar surface several times with its Chang'e programme and announces a crewed mission for the late 2020s. For Washington, Artemis is therefore also a response to Beijing's space ambitions and the question of who will set the rules for using lunar resources such as water ice and helium-3.

European participation through ESA and industrial partners such as Airbus is strategically astute but structurally weak. Europe supplies technology yet has little influence over programme decisions. An independent European lunar strategy remains absent, a shortcoming increasingly significant given the growing commercial space market.

For a generation that grew up with the internet, Artemis has particular resonance: it is the first major collective project for the future presented to them as a horizon rather than a solution to a problem.

In Berlin, students finishing school held a party. The party was at the planetarium in Prenzlauer Berg. They made a lot of noise and left rubbish behind.

Afterwards, the students met again. They apologised. And they cleaned up the park. Many people thought this was good.

The headteacher was proud of his students. He said: It was a mistake, but their reaction was right. The teenagers took responsibility.

Last weekend, a school-leaving party at the planetarium in Berlin's Prenzlauer Berg got out of control. Several hundred students celebrated into the night, making noise, leaving lots of rubbish and damaging plants and benches in the park. Local residents called the police.

What happened next attracted positive attention: the classes organised their own action to make amends. The following Saturday, dozens of students came to the park with gloves and rubbish bags, cleaned up and apologised to park visitors.

A local resident told the Tagesspiegel he had been pleasantly surprised. The headteacher explained: The party was a mistake. But their willingness to make amends shows that these young people have learned to take responsibility.

What began as a typical neighbourhood complaint became a small lesson in responsibility and community. The school-leavers' party at the planetarium in Prenzlauer Berg had left its mark the previous weekend: destroyed flowerbeds, scattered rubbish and angry residents. Police were called and the party was broken up.

What followed was unusual: without prompting from school management or parents, the classes involved organised an action to make amends. Around sixty students arrived on Saturday with work gloves, repaired the damage and spoke with park visitors. Some brought handwritten apology cards.

The incident sheds interesting light on a generation frequently accused of having no sense of community. The students' reaction suggests the opposite: they made a mistake and corrected it in a way that went beyond the bare minimum.

The incident at Berlin's planetarium received more social media attention than expected, because of the response rather than the party. A group of young people independently organising an action to make amends without institutional pressure, and seeking public conversations with those affected, is remarkable when debate about the younger generation's values is so often shaped by sweeping judgements.

From a developmental psychology perspective, the event is instructive. Moral action rarely arises from instruction: it develops through experience, encountering consequences, and deciding to take responsibility even when nobody is watching. That is exactly what these students demonstrated. Their response was neither perfect nor unprompted by an incident, but it was real.

In an interview with the Tagesspiegel, the headteacher said he was proud but not surprised: in previous years, his students had learned that mistakes are part of life, and how one handles them says more about a person than the mistakes themselves.

That sounds banal. It is not.

A new study shows that many young people in Germany want to move to another country. Forty-one out of every hundred young people are thinking about it.

Why do they want to leave? There are not enough cheap homes. Jobs are often insecure. And many feel that politicians do not listen to them.

But many young people also stay in Germany. They love their family, their friends and their home country. Living abroad is a dream, but not for everyone.

According to the new 2026 youth study, one in five young Germans can seriously imagine leaving Germany permanently. Forty-one per cent at least do not rule it out. These are the highest figures since the survey began.

There are several reasons. Many mention high housing costs, especially in big cities. Others see better career opportunities or a more pleasant lifestyle abroad. Popular destinations include Canada, the Netherlands, Portugal and Scandinavian countries.

Experts warn of a brain drain: if well-educated young people leave Germany, they will later be missing as skilled workers. Politicians urgently need to improve living conditions for young people, particularly housing and political participation.

The figure is politically explosive: according to the 2026 youth study, 41 per cent of 14- to 29-year-olds in Germany can imagine living abroad in future. Even more alarming is that one in five is specifically planning it. Willingness to emigrate has increased by more than 15 percentage points compared with 2020.

The motives are complex. Housing comes first: in major cities such as Munich, Frankfurt and Berlin, affordable homes are barely available to young adults. Uncertain career prospects in changing industries and the feeling of living in a country that names problems without solving them add to the picture.

Economists warn of long-term consequences. Germany already faces a skilled labour shortage, and another wave of well-educated young emigrants would worsen it. The answer must go beyond appeals to structural policy: housing construction, wage development and genuine political participation.

When 41 per cent of an age cohort seriously considers leaving its country, this is no longer an individual phenomenon: it is a social diagnosis. The 2026 youth study suggests that a substantial part of the younger generation considers Germany's implicit social contract, that those who work and contribute will share in prosperity, to have been cancelled.

The causes are structural and cumulative. The housing crisis disproportionately affects young adults because they rarely benefit from inheritances and face the harshest conditions in the rental market. The labour market offers employment, but increasingly through project-based, temporary or platform-mediated arrangements that make planning difficult. Generational inequality in political representation adds to this: people under 30 are chronically underrepresented in parliaments and leadership positions.

Willingness to emigrate thus reflects rational calculation rather than global-mindedness or enthusiasm for mobility: those who are young and qualified have options. And those with options compare.

The real question is whether Germany is prepared to create conditions under which young people need not weigh up whether they want to stay, but simply want to.

In Germany, many students start their Abitur exams on 16 April. The Abitur is very important. It is the final school exam.

The exams are equally difficult for all students. There are exams in German, mathematics and English. Students have to study a lot.

After the Abitur, students can go to university or train for a job. Many families celebrate the Abitur. It is a big day for the family.

On Thursday, 16 April, the 2026 Abitur exams begin in North Rhine-Westphalia. More than 90,000 students are taking the Abitur this year. The first exam is in German.

There is an important change this year: for the first time, students may use digital tools in some subjects, but not AI programmes. The ministry wants to develop students' digital skills without machines taking over their work.

Many students are nervous but also proud. Schools have offered intensive preparation courses in recent weeks. Teachers recommend getting enough sleep, eating well and not panicking.

The 2026 Abitur exam period begins in North Rhine-Westphalia on 16 April. Around 92,000 students are sitting the exams, more than at any time in five years. Education experts attribute the increase to larger birth cohorts and greater participation in education.

A new feature this year is the limited permission to use digital devices in selected subjects. Spreadsheet programmes are permitted in mathematics and economics, for example, but all forms of AI-assisted text generation remain prohibited. The education ministry emphasises that independent work and critical thinking remain central.

However, critics complain that the rules are inconsistent and difficult for students to understand. Teachers' associations call for clearer nationwide guidelines, as the federal structure of Germany's education system leads to considerable differences between states.

As the 2026 Abitur exams begin in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's education system again faces the question of how to reconcile traditional performance expectations with the reality of a thoroughly digital society. Cautiously allowing digital tools in individual subjects is a tentative step, more experiment than reform.

The structural dilemma is familiar: while students routinely use AI tools in daily life, they must pretend these do not exist in the examination room. The Abitur's legitimacy as proof of readiness for university and employment requires the competencies measured to remain socially relevant, an assumption increasingly called into question.

For years, educational researchers have advocated redefining examination competencies: the emphasis should be on critical assessment, source verification and creative problem-solving rather than flawless reproduction of knowledge. Whether politicians are willing to fundamentally rethink the Abitur remains doubtful given federal fragmentation and political conservatism in education.

The 2026 Abitur is therefore not only an examination for students, but also a test of the system itself.

FC St. Pauli is a well-known football club in Hamburg. It is known for its special values: equality and solidarity. But the women's team has big problems.

There are not enough training grounds for the women. Money is also a problem. The men's team receives much more money than the women's team.

Many fans are sad. They ask: Can a club like St. Pauli be so unfair? The club must find a solution now.

FC St. Pauli is considered one of Germany's most progressive clubs. Anti-racism, feminism and solidarity are part of the Hamburg club's official identity. But the reality of its women's football section looks different.

The women's team trains on poor pitches and has almost no budget. At the same time, women's football is booming in Germany: the national team is reaching more fans, and the Bundesliga attracts larger audiences. St. Pauli seems to be missing this trend.

Fans and players are demanding more investment and better conditions. The club has announced improvements, but there are no concrete plans yet. Many see this as a contradiction of the values St. Pauli communicates publicly.

For decades, FC St. Pauli has presented itself as an alternative to commercialised professional sport: grassroots-democratic, feminist and anti-fascist. This makes the contrast with its own women's football section all the more striking. Despite Germany's women's football boom, it struggles with outdated infrastructure, a limited budget and a lack of public attention.

The potential exists: the club has a loyal, committed fan base supporting progressive values. Yet a gap separates declarations from structural investment, a pattern visible across German women's football. Even in the women's Bundesliga, players receive on average less than a tenth of their male colleagues' salaries.

Critics accuse the club of using feminism as a marketing tool without providing the necessary resources. Club management acknowledges the need for action but points to limited financial flexibility. A credible response is still lacking.

FC St. Pauli is a special case in German football, not only because of the skull-and-crossbones flags in the stands. Over decades, the club has built an image that inseparably links political positions with club identity. Anti-capitalism, queer inclusion and gender equality are part of a living fan culture rather than mere marketing promises.

Precisely for this reason, the structural disadvantage faced by the women's football section is particularly serious. While the club publicly champions equality, the women's team trains on pitches falling short of international standards and operates on a budget nowhere near comparable to the men's. This contradiction is the result of years of prioritisation decisions rather than chance.

The St. Pauli debate represents a wider social question: what does structural equality actually cost, and who is willing to pay? Germany's women's football boom, visible in steadily increasing audiences and media presence, offers an opportunity to readjust. Whether it is taken will be measured by budget allocations rather than declarations.

For FC St. Pauli, this is more than a sporting policy issue. It is a question of credibility.

Germany has new pension rules from 2026. People who earn a lot do not get a higher pension. This is the law.

A pension is money for older people. You receive a pension when you no longer work. The more you have worked, the more pension you get, but only up to a limit.

Many people in Germany worry about retirement. They ask: Will I have enough money when I am old? The government says the system is stable. But many people do not believe it.

New pension values apply in Germany from 2026. The current pension value rises slightly, meaning pensioners receive a little more money. However, there is also a clear limit: people whose income exceeds a certain level do not receive a higher pension.

Germany's pension system is complicated. Everyone who works pays part of their salary into the pension fund each month. Later, they receive this money back, but the amount depends on many factors: how long they worked, how much they earned and when they retire.

Experts warn that the system will face long-term problems. There are more and more older people and fewer young workers. The federal government is discussing various reforms, but a solution is not yet in sight.

Pension payments will rise by 3.74 per cent on 1 July 2026, an increase considered noticeable in real terms following the recent fall in inflation. A new income limit also comes into force: anyone earning above the pension ceiling acquires no additional pension entitlements, a politically controversial mechanism.

The demographic imbalance is central to the debate: Germany is ageing rapidly. By 2040, people over 67 will account for around 23 per cent of the total population. Meanwhile, the number of contributors is shrinking. This places structural pressure on the pay-as-you-go pension system.

The federal government has announced a pension package that includes a funded component. However, critics doubt whether the fund-based solution can be designed fairly and take effect in time to close the foreseeable financing gap.

Germany's annual pension adjustment is a political ritual: the figure is announced, the opposition criticises it as too small, the government praises it as a sign of stability, and the system's real problems remain untouched. The 3.74-per-cent increase on 1 July 2026 follows this pattern.

The structural challenge has been known for decades: the pay-as-you-go system, in which workers' contributions directly finance current pensions, requires a balanced age structure. Germany has long ceased to have one. The old-age dependency ratio, the relationship between pensioners and contributors, worsens annually while political reforms fail to keep pace with demographic reality.

The announced generational capital, a state-managed fund modelled on Scandinavian approaches, is conceptually reasonable, but arrives too late and on too small a scale to close the foreseeable funding gap in the 2030s. Distribution is another problem: a funded component systematically favours those already holding private savings.

The pension system needs an honest social debate about lifetime working hours, immigration as a demographic resource, and what solidarity between generations means in the twenty-first century, rather than another adjustment package.

There was a fire at a hospital in Aachen on Tuesday. The hospital is called Alexianer. The fire service arrived quickly.

The fire was big. But the patients were safe. The nurses did a good job. Nobody died.

The fire service put out the fire. Afterwards, the police investigated why it started. The hospital now needs repairs.

A fire broke out at the Alexianer psychiatric clinic in Aachen on Tuesday morning. The fire service responded with a large team: more than 80 emergency workers were at the scene. The fire was put out after around two hours.

Thanks to the nursing staff's quick action, all patients were evacuated in time. Nobody was seriously injured. Aachener Zeitung journalist Kian Tabatabaei, who was at the scene, reported a calm and professional evacuation.

The cause has not yet been fully established. Police have opened an investigation. The affected wing remains closed until further notice. Clinic management thanked the emergency services for their quick response.

A major fire at the Alexianer psychiatric clinic in Aachen triggered a large fire service operation on Tuesday morning. Around 85 emergency workers responded after smoke was reported from the building's north wing at about 10:30. The fire was brought under control after approximately two hours.

The patient population made the situation especially delicate: the psychiatric clinic houses people who rely on guidance and support. Nevertheless, evacuation was orderly. Staff had regularly completed fire drills, a circumstance explicitly highlighted by fire service spokesperson Thomas Hensel.

Property damage is estimated at several hundred thousand euros. The cause remains under investigation; arson has not been ruled out. The affected wing will stay closed until cleared by the building authority, and patients have been accommodated in other parts of the clinic.

Tuesday's major fire at Aachen's Alexianer clinic ended without serious consequences, thanks to a quick fire service response, well-trained staff and apparently functioning evacuation plans. However, the operation raises questions beyond this individual case: how well are Germany's psychiatric facilities prepared for fire scenarios?

The answer is not straightforward. While large clinics such as Alexianer can demonstrate regular fire drills, smaller psychiatric facilities and care homes often lack staffing resources for systematic emergency preparation. This is structurally problematic because evacuation in psychiatry poses particular challenges: patients may be disoriented, slowed by medication or experiencing acute crises.

The cause remains under investigation. Arson has not been ruled out, highlighting another vulnerability rarely discussed publicly: internal security. Tensions between therapeutic freedom and the duty of protection, and between open wards and security requirements, are structurally inherent in psychiatry.

The Aachen fire cost no lives. Nevertheless, it should prompt us to stop taking fire safety in sensitive facilities for granted.

El Niño is a weather phenomenon in the Pacific. Warm ocean water changes the weather around the world. In some years, El Niño is very strong.

Scientists say El Niño could be very strong again in 2026. This means Europe could become very hot and dry. There could also be more storms.

People should prepare. Drinking more water, protecting nature and saving energy are important actions. The climate is changing, and we must deal with it.

Scientists are warning of a strong El Niño event in 2026. El Niño is a warming of the Pacific Ocean that affects weather worldwide. Changes in winds and ocean currents suggest the phenomenon could be especially intense this year.
