For Europe, this means higher temperatures, less rain and a greater risk of forest fires in summer. Southern Europe is particularly affected, but Germany and its neighbours also feel the effects. Last April, with its record temperatures, could be an early sign.

Climate researchers stress that El Niño alone is not responsible for warming. Human-caused climate change further strengthens the effects. Governments and citizens should prepare for a hot summer now.

Oceanographic measurements indicate a stronger El Niño event in the second half of 2026. Surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific are already well above the long-term average, a pattern climate models associate with a higher likelihood of extremely hot summers in parts of Europe.

El Niño changes atmospheric circulation patterns, potentially causing drought in the Mediterranean and altered rainfall patterns in central Europe. These effects are intensified when combined with existing climate change, something scientists call a climate amplification effect.

Agriculture and water supplies in Germany are particularly at risk. The German Weather Service has announced that it will activate its heat early warning systems well in advance. Whether political and infrastructure preparations are sufficient will become clear in summer.

El Niño is not a new phenomenon: South American fishermen described the irregular warming of the equatorial Pacific as early as the nineteenth century. What has changed is the context: in a world 1.3 degrees warmer, El Niño produces different, generally more extreme effects than in pre-industrial times.

Current measurements are troubling. Oceanographic buoys in the Pacific record deviations from average levels comparable to strong historical El Niño events such as 1997/98 and 2015/16, which caused severe droughts in East Africa, floods in South America and European heatwaves. Models from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research predict an above-average probability of extreme temperatures in central Europe in summer 2026.

The scientific difficulty lies in attribution: which specific extreme events result from El Niño, which from human-caused climate change, and where do the two reinforce each other? Attribution research has made considerable progress in recent years: it can now establish with high statistical confidence how much climate change has increased the likelihood of a particular event.

What remains is the political question: how does a society prepare for extreme weather expected to become increasingly frequent and intense? The answer cannot be purely meteorological. It must address infrastructure, society and, ultimately, democracy.

Petrol currently costs a lot of money in Germany. The price is at a record high. Many people have to pay more when they drive.

This is why more and more people are buying an electric car. An electric car does not need petrol. It only needs electricity. This is cheaper.

The federal government wants more people to buy electric cars. The government gives money for new electric cars. Many car brands have new electric models.

Petrol and diesel prices in Germany reached a new high in April 2026. A litre of premium petrol costs more than 2.10 euros at many filling stations. Consumers particularly notice this when commuting and on long journeys.

High fuel prices have a direct consequence: demand for electric cars is rising. Around 18 per cent more electric cars were sold in Germany in the first quarter of 2026 than in the same period last year. Cheaper models from Germany and China are particularly popular.

Experts say the trend will continue if charging infrastructure keeps improving. Many rural areas currently still lack enough charging stations. The federal government has announced an expansion programme to create one million public charging points by 2027.

In April 2026, Germany is experiencing its highest fuel prices since records began. A litre of premium petrol costs a national average of 2.14 euros, with diesel slightly below. The cause is a combination of global raw material shortages, the continuing geopolitical situation in the Middle East and carbon pricing, which rose again at the beginning of the year.

The economic burden on commuters is considerable: someone travelling 30 kilometres to work each day now spends around 180 euros monthly on petrol alone. This increases pressure to switch to emission-free alternatives. New electric vehicle registrations rose by 18.4 per cent in the first quarter, with electric cars outselling diesels for the first time.

Nevertheless, the electric car market's expansion remains fragile. Charging infrastructure in disadvantaged regions is still incomplete, and many households cannot afford purchase costs even with government support. So far, the shift to electric mobility has mainly taken place among higher-income urban households.

Record fuel prices in April 2026 have reignited a familiar debate: are high energy prices the most effective tool for accelerating the mobility transition, or primarily a burden on low-income households dependent on cars and unable to switch to electric mobility quickly?

As so often in climate policy, the answer is complex in distributive terms. For someone living in a well-connected city, with sufficient income and a garage offering charging facilities, high fuel prices provide a rational incentive to switch. For commuters lacking these conditions, the same prices simply increase costs without an alternative.

Registration figures reflect this picture: growth in electric cars is concentrated in major cities and prosperous regions. In disadvantaged rural districts, the electric share stagnates while the transport burden from expensive fuel grows. A mobility transition deepening this division is not socially sustainable.

What is missing is a comprehensive policy combining pricing tools with infrastructure investment, expanded public transport and targeted social compensation. Without this framework, the transport transition remains a project for the privileged.

SC Freiburg is a football club from Baden-Württemberg. It plays in the Europa League. This is an important competition in Europe.

On 9 April, Freiburg played against Celta Vigo from Spain. It was the first leg of the quarter-final. Many fans watched the match in the stadium and on television.

Freiburg is a small club, but it plays very well. The fans are very proud. The match was exciting and important for the next round.

SC Freiburg played the first leg of its Europa League quarter-final against Spanish club Celta Vigo on Wednesday evening. The match took place at Freiburg's Europa-Park Stadion and was broadcast live on RTL.

This is a historic season for SC Freiburg: for only the second time, the club has qualified for a European quarter-final. Particular attention focused on 20-year-old talent Johan Manzambi, whose strong performances have attracted attention this season.

The return match takes place in Vigo in two weeks. Freiburg is considered the outsider but has repeatedly shown this season that it can compete with big clubs. Fans across the region are following eagerly.

The kick-off against Celta Vigo opened another chapter in SC Freiburg's remarkable European history. The Europa League quarter-final first leg was significant for the Baden-based Bundesliga club both competitively and financially: reaching the semi-final would bring millions in revenue, allowing further structural development.

Johan Manzambi was once again the centre of attention. At 20, with twelve goals and seven assists this season, he is the outstanding player in coach Julian Brechtel's squad. Several leading European clubs have reportedly expressed interest, but Freiburg is keeping its young star for now.

The club symbolises a model considered almost anachronistic in modern football economics: sound budgeting, youth development rather than transfer madness, and continuity in the coaching team. That this model produces European quarter-finals is a strong argument for those sceptical of football dominated by money.

For SC Freiburg, the Europa League quarter-final is more than a sporting event. It is the current high point of a club project representing a structural alternative in European football's increasingly finance-dominated world, raising a question that extends beyond sport: are sustainable management and sporting success compatible?

The figures suggest that under certain conditions they are. For years, Freiburg has operated one of the Bundesliga's most efficient youth academies, kept staff costs low relative to revenue and treated coaching continuity as a competitive advantage. The outcome is the fruit of institutional patience increasingly rare in modern football, rather than coincidence.

Twenty-year-old Johan Manzambi exemplifies this approach: developed in the club's academy, deliberately supported, and now performing internationally. His market value is estimated at more than 40 million euros. The club faces a decision familiar to almost every Bundesliga side: sell and fund further development, or retain and take a risk.

Freiburg's performance this season is not a blueprint for everyone, but it proves structural intelligence can compete without petrodollars, at least up to a point.

Many children and teenagers in Germany use their phones a lot. Sometimes too much. This is called phone addiction.

Phone addiction is a problem. Children sleep badly, study less and meet friends less often. Their parents are worried.

Experts say you should not use your phone for more than two hours a day. And in the evening, you should put it away early. This is healthy.

A new study by the Federal Centre for Health Education shows that more than a third of teenagers in Germany aged 12 to 17 show signs of problematic smartphone use. On average, they reach for their phones every seven minutes, even at night.

The consequences are clear: lack of sleep, poorer school results and fewer social contacts in the real world. Social media apps and video platforms are particularly responsible for long usage times. Their algorithms are designed to hold attention for as long as possible.

Many parents do not know how to discuss the issue. Experts recommend agreed rules rather than bans, phone-free mealtimes and no screens in bedrooms. Schools should give media literacy a stronger place in lessons.

The Federal Centre for Health Education's latest survey paints a worrying picture: 34 per cent of Germany's 12- to 17-year-olds meet criteria indicating problematic smartphone use. Teenagers spend more than five hours daily on their devices on average, a considerable portion after midnight.

The psychological effects are well documented: sleep disorders, increased anxiety, reduced concentration and weaker real-world social bonds. Particularly problematic is the variable reinforcement used by social media algorithms: unpredictable rewards, such as likes, new content and notifications, activate the same neurological reward system as gambling.

Prevention programmes encounter structural obstacles in practice. Schools have little time for media literacy lessons, and many parents feel overwhelmed. Some federal states are discussing legal restrictions for under-16s, following countries such as France and Australia.

The debate about teenagers' phone addiction suffers from a fundamental framing distortion: it is often treated as a question of individual self-control or parental supervision, while the structural causes, the deliberate engineering of maximum user engagement by technology companies, remain in the background.

The mechanisms are familiar and well researched. Variable reinforcement, infinite scrolling, personalised content feeds and algorithmic escalation of emotional material form digital platforms' commercial foundation rather than incidental by-products. They are designed to monopolise attention and work particularly effectively on teenagers, because the prefrontal cortex responsible for impulse control does not fully mature until around age 25.

Against this background, calls for greater media literacy fall short because they ignore the asymmetry between individual users and institutionalised behavioural engineers. A 13-year-old is expected to develop cognitive resilience against systems whose design incorporates investment by teams of behavioural economists and neuroscientists.

What is missing is regulation holding platform providers accountable: age verification, transparent algorithms and default usage limits for minors. This means establishing market rules in an area producing clear negative externalities, rather than paternalism.

There is a ceasefire between the US and Iran. This means the two countries are not fighting at the moment. This is good news.

The war caused problems for German companies. It was difficult to sell goods to other countries. This is called exporting.

Now many German companies hope things will improve again. But experts say it will take more time.

The ceasefire between the US and Iran agreed in late March 2026 has given German companies hope. The war, which began on 28 February, had seriously affected global trade, especially through the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important shipping routes.

However, the Federation of German Wholesale, Foreign Trade and Services, BGA, expects the economic consequences to remain noticeable for some time. Many contracts were cancelled, supply chains interrupted and insurance premiums for sea freight sharply increased.

The Federal Statistical Office released new data on German exports in February 2026: they were 8.3 per cent below the previous year's level. Industries such as engineering, chemicals and automotive are particularly affected. A quick recovery is possible but not guaranteed.

The ceasefire agreed between the US and Iran on 28 March has temporarily eased the most immediate threat to global trade routes. The Strait of Hormuz, through which around 20 per cent of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas transport passes, is navigable again, a development that has already stabilised international energy markets.

For Germany's export economy, the easing comes at a critical moment. The 8.3-per-cent year-on-year drop in foreign revenue in February 2026 abruptly interrupted the economic recovery emerging since autumn 2025. Engineering and the chemical industry in particular report order postponements worth billions.

However, the BGA warns against premature optimism. A ceasefire is not a peace treaty, and the Middle East's geopolitical situation remains structurally unstable. Companies seeking more resilient supply chains should not treat the current pause as a reason to abandon diversification.

The ceasefire in the Iran conflict again illustrates a structural vulnerability in Germany's economic model: its deep dependence on open trade routes, stable supply chains and geopolitical predictability. The 8.3-per-cent export decline in February 2026 is not statistical noise but a symptomatic expression of the costs an export-oriented economy bears when geopolitical order becomes fragile.

Germany exports around 47 per cent of its gross domestic product, a figure with few international parallels. This export strength is historically the foundation of German prosperity, but also its greatest systemic risk. Concentration on a few key markets and global value chains spanning continents leaves the country vulnerable to shocks over which it has little influence.

The economic policy response has so far been hesitant. Nearshoring and supply chain resilience have long been familiar concepts, but implementation is costly and slow. Economic and security interests also do not always align: excessive decoupling from risky regions weakens the domestic economic base, while excessive integration increases geopolitical vulnerability.

The ceasefire gives Germany breathing space, not a solution. How an export-dependent economy can become structurally more resilient in an age of geopolitical fragmentation remains an urgent, unanswered question.
